stories.topic: Why Do We Fight? (The Pre-Show Fumble)
stories.summary: The episode opens with Amit and Ajay fumbling about who should speak first — neither wanting to go, both wanting the other to. Amit uses the meta-moment to launch the episode's thesis: we tell simple stories to make sense of a deeply complex world, and we fight because our stories don't coordinate, or because both stories are wrong and conflict with reality itself. Our instincts were forged for prehistoric tribes, and many no longer match the world we live in.
stories.insight: Fights are rarely about facts; they're about mismatched simple stories laid over a complex world. Naming the mismatch is the first step out of it.

stories.topic: The Direction of the Wind (Bones-on-Ribs at Ferguson College)
stories.summary: In late-1980s Ferguson College Pune, Amit was so thin you could count his ribs. After a boys' school, he found himself in an arts class that was 80% girls, and his daily heuristic for which exit to take from class — canteen or tapri — was the direction of the wind, so his shirt wouldn't blow against his chest and reveal the ribs. Gyms weren't yet part of the culture; he had no idea what to do.
stories.insight: A small, warming snapshot of adolescent self-consciousness — and a setup for the post-hoc punchline that follows. The earnestness of the heuristic makes it stick.

stories.topic: Ryan, Push-Ups, and the Post-Hoc Fallacy
stories.summary: Amit's friend Ryan, also extremely thin, was a devout Christian. One day Amit caught him doing push-ups behind a closed door — a violation of the unspoken thin-boys' code. Ryan's explanation: masturbation was a sin, and he had decreed twenty-five push-ups per occurrence as penance. Six months later Ryan walked through campus as a Greek god while girls giggled. Then their friend Varun came to Amit asking how to get a body like Ryan's. Amit, deliberately, gave him the post-hoc answer: 'You have to masturbate.'
stories.insight: A perfect, unforgettable illustration of post hoc ergo propter hoc. Two things happened in sequence; therefore the first caused the second. Religion, superstition, and most folk-economics are powered by the same wiring.

stories.topic: The Witch Doctor's Coat and the Flooding Nile
stories.summary: Every spring, the witch doctor takes off his coat. Then the Nile floods. The witch doctor claims his coat caused the flood. Functionally the sequence is correct — first spring, then coat, then flood — but attributing causality to the coat is absurd. Ajay extends this with a thought experiment: if pressing a button delivers a biscuit one second later, the human mind locks in causality instantly; make the delay ten hours and we're cognitively lost.
stories.insight: Our cause-and-effect circuitry is tuned to short timescales. The longer the lag between an action and its consequence, the worse our intuition gets — which is why so much of policy, climate, health, and life requires deliberate, evidence-based reasoning rather than gut.

stories.topic: Don Boudreaux's Coin in the Crowded Pool
stories.summary: A metaphor Amit borrows (via Shruti Rajagopalan) from Don Boudreaux. To test whether dropping a coin raises water level: in a controlled lab beaker, trivial. Now do the same experiment in an enormous crowded swimming pool, with people splashing, wind blowing, rain falling. The data you extract will be garbage. Most social science lives in the swimming pool, not the lab.
stories.insight: Causation in the social world is almost never cleanly recoverable. The honest response is humility and caution — not faux-rigour layered over noisy data, and not confirmation bias dressed as conclusion.

stories.topic: The Monkey, the Darts, and the Infosys IPO
stories.summary: In finance, a well-accepted result: a monkey throwing darts at a stock list builds a portfolio that beats 99.9% of clever humans trying to pick stocks. Ajay extends this to industry choice: when the Infosys IPO happened in 1994, it was undersubscribed because nobody knew the Indian software industry was about to explode. People who got rich in software tend to attribute the wealth to their own decisions, but the right baseline is: 'If I had bought ten random companies in this industry and done nothing, how would I have fared?' Anything above that is your contribution; everything else is dumb luck of being in the right industry.
stories.insight: Strip out the industry tailwind before crediting the CEO. About 98% of what happens to any of us is luck — neither getting cocky on success nor crushed on failure is the right response. Focus on processes, not narratives about your own greatness.

stories.topic: The Tomato Glut and the Chip Glut
stories.summary: There's a shortage of tomatoes, so a farmer reasons: 'I'll plant tomatoes and make a fortune.' Sensible — for one. But a million farmers reason the same way, and next season there's a glut, the price collapses to zero, and angry farmers tip truckfuls of tomatoes onto the road because transport isn't worth it. Same pattern with semiconductors: a global chip shortage triggers a wave of new fabs, and within a year or two the world will see chip-maker bankruptcies from the resulting oversupply.
stories.insight: The fallacy of composition operationalised. What is rational for one is often disastrous when scaled — and good economic reasoning means asking, every time, 'What happens if everyone does this?'

recommendations.item: Economic Facts and Fallacies
recommendations.creator: Thomas Sowell
recommendations.context: The book whose opening chapters lay out the five foundational fallacies that frame this episode.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls Sowell one of his intellectual heroes and uses the book as the spine of this episode. Sowell sets out fallacies that aren't just errors but generative — many other errors descend from them — and argues that becoming a better thinker requires understanding our own hardwired frailties.

recommendations.item: The Double 'Thank You' Moment
recommendations.creator: John Stossel
recommendations.context: Stossel's column on the small ritual of buying coffee — both sides say thank you because both are better off.
recommendations.reason: The cleanest possible refutation of the zero-sum fallacy. Voluntary transactions leave both parties better off; the world is positive-sum, and the explosion of double-thank-you moments after the Industrial Revolution is the engine of modern prosperity.

recommendations.item: Why Freedom Matters (Episode 10, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: An earlier EIE episode that traced the history of human prosperity.
recommendations.reason: Source of the famous flat-then-vertical world GDP chart — flat for centuries, then exploding with the Industrial Revolution and the spread of free markets. The chart is the visual proof of the positive-sum world.

recommendations.item: Profit = Philanthropy
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's column reframing the pursuit of profit.
recommendations.reason: Amit's argument that in a world of voluntary transactions, the only way to make a profit is by making someone else better off — making profit, properly understood, the greatest form of philanthropy.

recommendations.item: The Great Redistribution
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's column setting out 'Varma's Law.'
recommendations.reason: Source of 'Varma's Law' — most state interference in free markets ends up redistributing wealth from the poor to the rich (e.g. tariffs, where consumers pay more and the gains accrue to narrow protected interest groups). A useful corrective to the assumption that intervention helps the weak.

recommendations.item: The Evolution of Cooperation
recommendations.creator: Robert Axelrod
recommendations.context: Axelrod's classic on the iterated prisoner's dilemma and the emergence of cooperation.
recommendations.reason: Formalises optimal response to misbehaviour: strike back once, but not twice, not thrice, not forever. Don't let it go, but don't bear a grudge — the warlike-tribe response is suboptimal even on its own terms. The book Ajay leans on for the architecture of good norms.

recommendations.item: Tim Urban's Tweet on Getting to Know People
recommendations.creator: Tim Urban
recommendations.context: A Wait But Why tweet about meeting humans on either tail of one's expectations.
recommendations.reason: 'Whenever I get to know someone who seems perfect, I end up disappointed. Whenever I get to know someone who I think is the worst of the worst, I'm pleasantly surprised. Angels and demons aren't real.' A vivid expression of regression to the mean as applied to character — and an antidote to the social-media flip of the fallacy of composition that paints whole groups in one colour.

recommendations.item: The Day Ryan Started Masturbating
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's written-up version of the Ryan-and-the-push-ups story.
recommendations.reason: The full piece behind the post-hoc parable from this episode.

recommendations.item: Wet Streets Cause Rain (the Gell-Mann Amnesia passage)
recommendations.creator: Michael Crichton
recommendations.context: Crichton's name for the reverse-causation fallacy.
recommendations.reason: The crisp Crichton coinage Amit uses to label the inversion of post hoc — getting the causal arrow upside-down. Doubles as Crichton's famous Gell-Mann Amnesia setup.

recommendations.item: The Forgotten Man
recommendations.creator: Amity Shlaes
recommendations.context: Shlaes's revisionist economic history of the Great Depression.
recommendations.reason: Backs Sowell's claim that the 1929 crash didn't cause the Depression — government interventions (Smoot-Hawley and the rest) did. A useful counter to the standard textbook story that bakes in a post-hoc fallacy.

recommendations.item: Poker and Life (Episode 38, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: An earlier EIE episode on probability, luck, and decision-making.
recommendations.reason: The episode where the 98%-luck idea was developed at length. Don't judge a decision by its outcome; the world is probabilistic; focus on processes and good algorithms rather than self-congratulation or self-flagellation.

recommendations.item: The Man of System (excerpt from The Theory of Moral Sentiments)
recommendations.creator: Adam Smith
recommendations.context: Smith's passage on the planner who imagines society as a chessboard.
recommendations.reason: The ur-text of the chess-pieces fallacy. Smith's 'man of system' arranges human beings as if they were pieces on a board, forgetting that each piece has its own principle of motion. Two and a half centuries on, still the cleanest indictment of central planning.

recommendations.item: The Fatal Conceit: The Errors of Socialism
recommendations.creator: Friedrich Hayek
recommendations.context: Hayek's late book on the limits of designed social order.
recommendations.reason: The other classic statement of the chess-pieces fallacy — Hayek's 'fatal conceit' is the belief that we can engineer society from the top down. We can't: we don't have the data, the information, or the capacity to handle the complexity.

recommendations.item: The Use of Knowledge in Society
recommendations.creator: Friedrich Hayek
recommendations.context: Hayek's 1945 American Economic Review essay on dispersed knowledge.
recommendations.reason: Source of the spontaneous-order argument: real-world knowledge is dispersed across millions of minds, prices aggregate it, and no central planner can possibly outperform the distributed system.

recommendations.item: Four Papers That Changed the World (Episode 41, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: An earlier EIE episode on world-changing economics papers, including Hayek's.
recommendations.reason: The deep-dive treatment of Hayek's knowledge-in-society argument and spontaneous order, referenced here as essential prerequisite reading for the chess-pieces fallacy.

recommendations.item: The Selfish Gene
recommendations.creator: Richard Dawkins
recommendations.context: Dawkins's classic on gene-level natural selection.
recommendations.reason: Ajay's reach for why top-down control fails 'all the way down': the monkey on the prairie was optimising for herself, and you can never push out the energy and zeal of each individual pursuing their own life, liberty, and happiness. Every centrally planned model collapses against this.

recommendations.item: Untitled (a poem)
recommendations.creator: Leonard Cohen
recommendations.context: A Cohen poem, used as the epigraph to the technology-policy chapter of In Service of the Republic.
recommendations.reason: A slave's voice telling the master that any system designed without us will not stand. A reminder that policy designed over the heads of the people it acts on is fragile by design.

recommendations.item: In Service of the Republic: The Art and Science of Economic Policy
recommendations.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Kelkar and Shah's book on Indian economic policy.
recommendations.reason: The Leonard Cohen poem appears as an epigraph to its technology-policy chapter; the book also develops the no-free-lunch and coercive-power arguments that frame the open-ended fallacy section.

recommendations.item: Understanding the State (Episode 25, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: An earlier EIE episode on the nature of state power.
recommendations.reason: The episode that develops the idea that every act of government is an act of coercion — the prerequisite for understanding the no-free-lunch implication of the open-ended fallacy.

recommendations.item: When Should the State Act? (Episode 26, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: An earlier EIE episode pairing with Episode 25.
recommendations.reason: Develops the two big constraints on policy: the budget constraint (spending trade-offs) and the more dangerous absence of any equivalent constraint on coercive power.

recommendations.item: The Economics and Politics of Vaccines (Episode 223, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Amit's deep-dive Seen-and-the-Unseen episode with Ajay on health policy.
recommendations.reason: The detailed source for Ajay's contrarian-sounding plea — that a sophisticated Indian health expert should advocate cutting government healthcare spending and reorienting toward public-health prevention rather than curative healthcare.

recommendations.item: Declutter (Episode 30, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: An earlier EIE episode on simplifying one's life.
recommendations.reason: Where the personal application of the open-ended fallacy first surfaced — the time constraint shifts as you age, and prioritising means saying no to things you love, not just things you don't.

recommendations.item: Why We Fight: The Roots of War and the Paths to Peace
recommendations.creator: Christopher Blattman
recommendations.context: Blattman's book on the economics of violence.
recommendations.reason: Ajay's central recommendation. Blattman opens up violence as an object of economic analysis — both citizen-citizen and state-citizen violence — and treats taming it as essential to development. Ajay is delighted that an economist has finally taken this seriously.

recommendations.item: The Three Languages of Politics
recommendations.creator: Arnold Kling
recommendations.context: Kling's slim book on the three ideological tribes of US politics.
recommendations.reason: Amit's central recommendation. Progressives speak oppressor/oppressed; conservatives speak civilisation/barbarism; libertarians speak liberty/coercion. Cross-tribe argument fails because each side starts from a different first principle. To persuade, speak to the other side's value, not your own — the practical path past ideological talking-past.

recommendations.item: In My Tribe
recommendations.creator: Arnold Kling
recommendations.context: Kling's Substack newsletter.
recommendations.reason: Amit's complementary recommendation to the book — Kling continues to extend and refine the three-languages framework on the newsletter.

recommendations.item: What's Wrong With Indian Agriculture? (Episode 18, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: An earlier EIE episode on Indian agriculture.
recommendations.reason: Source of the tomato-glut illustration of the fallacy of composition — and a deep dive into the agricultural cycles that recur because of it.

recommendations.item: The Populist Playbook (Episode 42, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: An earlier EIE episode on populism.
recommendations.reason: Connects to the three-languages discussion via Ajay's wolves-and-sheep frame: the sheep come in three flocks with different values, but their overarching shared interest is not being trampled by the wolves.

recommendations.item: The Art of Clear Writing
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's writing course.
recommendations.reason: Amit's standing recommendation, plugged in the show-notes.

recommendations.item: The India Uncut Newsletter
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's Substack newsletter.
recommendations.reason: Plugged in the show notes — 'furiously active again' according to the description.

core_ideas.concept: The Triad of Disagreement: Facts, Values, Reasoning Engine
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's frame for why people disagree. We bring three things to any judgment: facts (data, evidence — corrupted by the human tendency to overweight personal experience), values (beliefs about what is good — partly birthright, partly muddled), and a reasoning engine that processes both. Disagreement traces to a difference in one of the three. The 'dreams of reason' is the hope that at least the engine can be a shared, universal substrate of logic, argument, and proof — a common ground we can build on.
core_ideas.quote: Maybe there are certain universal stories of logic, of argument, of proof which we can all agree on, and we can construct a socially shared notion of truth.

core_ideas.explanation: An instinct fitted to a hunter-gatherer world: when the tribe kills a deer, every chunk you eat is a chunk I can't have, so every interaction looks like a fixed pie. In the modern world this is false — voluntary transactions leave both parties better off (Stossel's 'double thank-you' moment). The zero-sum mindset drives most statism, most envy of the rich, and the conflation of inequality with poverty. Liberalisation since 1991 lifted hundreds of millions of Indians out of poverty even as inequality rose, because the world is positive-sum.
core_ideas.quote: The pursuit of profit is the greatest form of philanthropy. It's an incentive towards doing good for others.

core_ideas.concept: Culture as the Greatest Positive-Sum Game
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's extension of the zero-sum critique to the realm of ideas. Newton, the Magna Carta, the transistor — none of these were extracted from anyone; the inventors didn't profit at our expense, and the world rebuilt itself around the discoveries. Knowledge has 'mind-blowing positive externality': it spills over and inflects everything. Treating the world as a fixed pie ignores that the largest pie of all — accumulated human knowledge — is one we keep adding to.

Amit's named claim: most state interference in free markets ends up redistributing wealth from the poor to the rich. The cleanest example is tariffs — competition shrinks, consumers pay more or get less value, and the wealth they would have kept is redirected to the narrow interest groups that lobbied for the tariff. Generalisable beyond tariffs: most regulatory capture follows the same arrow.
core_ideas.quote: Most interference in free markets leads to a redistribution from the poor to the rich.

core_ideas.explanation: Sowell's definition: the belief that what is true of a part is true of the whole. A baseball fan can see better by standing — but if every fan stands, no one sees better. Politicians constantly help a particular group, industry, or state and present the benefits to them as if they were net benefits to society — when they're really just robbing Peter to pay Paul. The full diagnostic question is always: 'What if everybody does this?'
core_ideas.quote: What logicians call the fallacy of composition is a belief that what is true of a part is true of the whole.

core_ideas.concept: A Country Is Not a Company
core_ideas.explanation: Why business intuition fails when imported into government — Ajay flagging a future episode title. Two reasons. First, the fallacy of composition: scaling firm-level rationality to economy-level policy unleashes systemic effects that don't exist for the firm. Second, the poison of coercive power: a firm has almost none, a state has it as its core mechanism. Different problem, different toolkit; the successful businessman who turns policymaker often gets both wrong.

Post hoc ergo propter hoc — after this, therefore because of this. The witch doctor's spring coat-removal precedes the Nile flood; we're cooked to read causality into mere sequence. The cousin fallacy is cum hoc ergo propter hoc — when two things are simultaneous, we assume one causes the other. And Crichton's 'wet streets cause rain' fallacy is the inverted-arrow version. Religion, superstition, and bad economics all lean on this wiring. The instinct served us in a small information environment; it betrays us in a complex one.
core_ideas.quote: Briefly stated, the Gell-Mann Amnesia effect is as follows...

core_ideas.explanation: Press a button, get a biscuit one second later — the human mind locks in causality after two trials. Stretch the lag to ten seconds, then ten hours, and our cause-effect circuitry collapses. We are constitutionally weak at perceiving relationships that play out over long timescales — which is precisely the timescale of climate, health, child development, policy, and most of the things that matter most. The remedy is deliberate evidence-based reasoning, not gut.
core_ideas.quote: The human mind is congenitally unable to see cause and effect playing out across longer time scales.

core_ideas.concept: The Coin in the Crowded Pool
core_ideas.explanation: A metaphor (Boudreaux via Shruti Rajagopalan) for how hard causal inference is in social science. In a controlled lab beaker, asking whether a coin raises water level is trivial. In a vast, crowded swimming pool with people splashing, wind blowing, and rain falling, the data is garbage. Most economic and social-science questions live in the swimming pool, which is why economists love rare natural experiments — North/South Korea, East/West Germany — that come closest to the lab.

core_ideas.concept: The 98% Rule: Most of What Happens Is Luck
core_ideas.explanation: From poker, finance, and life. About 98% of what happens to any of us is dumb luck, including the industry we ended up in (Infosys IPO undersubscribed in 1994 because no one knew). The right baseline isn't 'how well did I do' but 'how well would I have done if I bought ten random companies in this industry and did nothing?' Anything above that baseline is your contribution. The lesson is symmetric: don't get cocky on success, don't get crushed on failure. Focus on processes, not outcome-based self-narratives.

core_ideas.concept: The Chess Pieces Fallacy (The Man of System)
core_ideas.explanation: Adam Smith's 'man of system' imagines society as pieces on a board, infinitely arrangeable to his design. Hayek called the same impulse 'the fatal conceit.' The truth is the opposite: every chess piece has its own principle of motion, its own incentives, its own knowledge. Top-down planning works in a tribe of ten but breaks down at the scale of a society — the planner has neither the data nor the cognitive bandwidth, and Hayek's spontaneous order outperforms every attempt to replace it. Millions of Indians stayed poor for decades because of this fallacy.

Sowell again: 'Many desirable things are advocated without regard to the most fundamental fact of economics, that resources are inherently limited and have alternative uses.' Health, safety, open space — who could be against any of them? But each is open-ended, and resources are not. India's biggest religion, Amit says, is government; we treat the state as a maa-baap with infinite money. There is no free lunch, every rupee of government spending comes from coercive taxation that has its own costs, and good policy requires pairing every spending proposal with a list of where to cut.
core_ideas.quote: Many desirable things are advocated without regard to the most fundamental fact of economics, that resources are inherently limited and have alternative uses.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's deepening of the open-ended fallacy. Government spending at least bumps into a budget — the state has only so much money. But the state's coercive power has no equivalent ceiling. The government can keep banning things, keep oppressing, keep whittling away freedoms with no fiscal stop sign. So we should be even more cautious about state actions that reduce freedom than about those that merely cost money.

Arnold Kling's frame for cross-tribe argument. Liberals/progressives speak the language of equality (oppressor/oppressed). Conservatives speak civilisation/barbarism. Libertarians and classical liberals speak liberty/coercion. Each tribe speaks from its own first principle, and arguments framed in your tribe's language bounce off the other tribes' ears. The way past gridlock is to recognise the other person's first principle — itself an act of recognising their humanity — and frame your argument inside their value, not yours.

core_ideas.concept: Pessimism of the Intellect, Optimism of the Will
core_ideas.explanation: Amit's borrowed credo, used to wrap the bleak content of the episode. Yes, the world is full of fallacies and the consequences are real and ugly; we keep fighting. But seeing what is wrong is not the same as giving up on it — we keep working. The episode's larger plea: in a doctor-engineer-MBA-accountant-lawyer India that has reduced knowledge to credentials, the lost art is thinking itself, and reviving it is something we can each choose to do.
core_ideas.quote: Pessimism of the intellect, optimism of the will.

core_ideas.concept: The Open-Ended Fallacy of the Self
core_ideas.explanation: Amit's personal extension. As we age, the binding constraint shifts from money to time. We act as if time were unlimited — the illusion of immortality, painful for non-believers to dispel — and try to give mind-space to X and Y and Z. Steve Jobs's advice to Jonathan Ive: learn to say no, especially to things you love, because at any moment there are seven you love and the only way to do any of them well is to drop five.
core_ideas.quote: Learn to say no to things that you love.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Amit on the pre-show fumble: 'Both of us wanted the other one to go first and we ended up kind of fighting over it. Not really a fight, but it's a good question. Why do we keep fighting?' — turning a recording-studio mishap into the episode's thesis statement.

Amit narrating the Ryan punchline: 'Six months later, Ryan is full body, he's like a Greek god... and now I am the only person whose bones are visible.' The post-hoc payoff: Varun comes asking for the body, and Amit, deadpan, tells him the answer is masturbation.
Amit, mid-Ryan story, on Indian English: 'In my mind I did Shashtang Pranam and I just left.'
Amit on his keto diet during the biscuit thought experiment: 'I'm on a keto diet, so if I press a button, I don't want a biscuit to come ever. Bacon strips, another matter.'

Amit naming an economic law after himself: 'I'm going to a little vain. I'm going to name a law of economics after myself because I keep talking about it and no one seems to get it.' — christens 'Varma's Law' on air.
Amit on optimism vs Ajay's pessimism: 'See how optimistic Amit is. He says we have learned this lesson in India.' Ajay's reply: 'I worry that... you and I have learned this lesson.'

Amit's defence: 'I wasn't whining and we will fight over this — the use of your word whining. I don't whine. I just don't.' A small in-podcast loop where the host objects to being called a whiner and immediately starts whining about it.
Amit teasing Ajay on academic sociopaths: 'We know many economists who are sociopaths, Ajay, I want to tell you that. But I know you're not one of them.'

Amit, riffing on the 'great example of the Great Depression' slip: catches himself mid-sentence and laughs at how language messes with us — a casual, in-flight demonstration of the Freudian undertow in everyday speech.
Kumar Anand's coinage 'PPP — Perpetually Planned Poverty,' invoked as the consequence of zero-sum statism.
'Maa-baap sarkar' — the parent-state, invoked as the Indian default attitude that gives the open-ended fallacy its grip.
Adam Ferguson on social order: 'human action but not human design' — the original phrase for spontaneous order, invoked alongside Hayek.
Milton Friedman's 'no free lunch' — invoked as the canonical statement of the open-ended fallacy: every rupee of government spending comes from somewhere.
'Pessimism of the intellect, optimism of the will' — Antonio Gramsci's phrase, used as the episode's emotional resolution.
Tim Urban (Wait But Why) on regression-to-the-mean in human character: 'Angels and demons aren't real.'
Robert Trivers — invoked alongside Axelrod as the architect of the modern theory of reciprocal altruism: self-interest and altruism are not opposed but co-wired.
